What is PCA?
Rotate one line through a measured cloud. Watch four observations become four scores.
PCA finds new perpendicular axes, ordered by variance. Keeping fewer axes reduces the number of values per observation.
One number is a position on a line
Select an observation. Link its point, projection, and single stored score.
The point and its score refer to the same observation.
Some views lose more than others
Compare 45° and 135° with the same scale in both score plots.
A useful projection keeps a large part of the original squared spread.
A projection follows a perpendicular
Move one point to its closest position on the chosen line.
The line is the axis that we KEEP; the viewing direction is perpendicular to it.
What does one score lose?
Hide the original points. Reveal the possible points that share a score.
A score cannot recover movement across its axis.
Turn the axes, then remove one
Switch between two rotated coordinates and one retained coordinate.
Rotation alone loses nothing. Removing a coordinate can lose detail.
What will best mean?
Compare kept squared spread with squared reconstruction error.
These are two equivalent PCA objectives under the same Euclidean scale.
See the whole method once
Step through center → find axes → keep scores → reconstruct.
The next chapters explain how to compute this result.
Measure change from a shared center
Translate the cloud without changing its shape.
The PCA direction describes variation around the mean.
Find the center of this cloud
Highlight one column and calculate its mean.
Introduce the mean only because we need this center.
Move the center to zero
Scrub the translation. Keep observation labels fixed.
Subtract the corresponding feature mean from each observation.
The distances do not change
Select two observations before and after translation.
Centering changes the origin, not the relative positions.
Describe the line with two numbers
Rotate a unit arrow. Its horizontal and vertical parts update.
The vector w gives a direction and has length one.
Calculate one score
Select A. Multiply each centered coordinate by its direction weight.
The dot product gives signed distance along a unit axis.
Use one rule for every observation
Link each row of Xc to its score in Xc w.
Rows are observations; columns are features. Show the matrix shapes here.
Keep the ruler length fixed
Double the direction length without changing its angle.
Without the unit constraint, scores and variance can grow without limit.
How spread out are the scores?
Compare scores around zero at two angles.
Centered input produces scores whose mean is zero.
Signs cancel; squares do not
Switch signed contributions to square areas.
Squaring measures both directions and supports the distance identity used later.
Give spread a number
Add four squared scores and divide by three.
Use sample variance throughout. An optional note explains n−1; changing it to n does not change the best axis.
Search with a variance curve
Rotate the line. Link the angle to a point on the variance curve.
The highest point gives our numerical target. We still need a general method.
Open one squared score
Reveal each term in (w1 a + w2 b)².
Show the two identical cross-products before replacing them with a factor of two.
Add the same terms across rows
Select one observation in the sum. Then group matching terms.
The weights are shared by all observations, so they can leave the sum.
Two familiar sums and one new sum
Link the first and last terms to the two feature variances.
The middle sum measures how the two centered features vary together.
Build covariance from signed products
Select observations in each quadrant. Flip the second feature.
Same signs give positive products; opposite signs give negative products.
Variance alone cannot tell the tilt
Compare two clouds with the same marginal variances and opposite covariance.
The cross-term distinguishes these clouds.
Store the three quantities in S
Select a covariance matrix entry to reveal its products.
The diagonal stores variances. Both off-diagonal entries store the same covariance.
Compute S with one matrix product
Animate a selected row of Xcᵀ meeting a column of Xc.
Transpose and multiplication are compact ways to do the sums we already used.
Read wᵀ S w from inside out
Calculate Sw, then the dot product with w.
The compact formula is exactly the expanded variance expression.
Check both routes with real numbers
Compare direct squared scores with wᵀ S w at any angle.
The two calculations agree because we derived their identity.
State the optimization problem
Show a unit circle of permitted directions and a variance curve.
Maximize wᵀ S w with wᵀ w = 1.
What does S do to an arrow?
Move w around the unit circle. Show Sw on a common labeled scale.
A matrix is also a rule that maps one vector to another.
At an optimum, turning cannot help
Compare a direction with small clockwise and counterclockwise turns.
The allowed change runs along the circle. At an optimum its first-order gain is zero.
Find the variance slope
Differentiate the two-coordinate quadratic one term at a time.
The gradient is (2S11w1+2S12w2, 2S12w1+2S22w2) = 2Sw.
Find the constraint direction
Differentiate w1²+w2². Show the normal arrow to the circle.
The gradient 2w points outward; allowed small changes point perpendicular to it.
Match the two normal directions
Align the gradient arrows at a stationary point.
2Sw = 2λw, so Sw = λw. This finds candidates; it does not yet prove a maximum.
Name the equation after it appears
Compare w and Sw at both stationary directions.
An eigenvector keeps its direction under S. Its eigenvalue is the scale factor.
Find the possible scale factors
Subtract λ on the diagonal. Expand the 2×2 determinant.
A nonzero solution requires S−λI to be singular. Explain determinant only here.
Solve our two eigenvalues
Factor (10/3−λ)²−(8/3)². Link each root to the curve.
The roots are 6 and 2/3.
Find and normalize the directions
Solve w2=w1 and w2=−w1. Set each vector length to one.
The directions are (1,1)/√2 and (1,−1)/√2.
A candidate can be a minimum
Select each eigenvector and compare its variance.
The eigenvector equation alone does not choose PC1.
Why are these directions perpendicular?
Expand q1ᵀSq2 in two ways and compare.
Symmetry gives (λ1−λ2)q1ᵀq2=0. Distinct eigenvalues imply perpendicular eigenvectors.
Build any unit direction from them
Rotate w and show coefficients a and b on the two eigenvectors.
w=aq1+bq2 and a²+b²=1. State the symmetric-matrix basis theorem for higher dimensions.
Expand variance in the new basis
Open four terms. Cancel both cross-terms with orthogonality.
The result is λ1a²+λ2b².
Prove the largest value wins
Move the squared-weight allocation between λ1 and λ2.
A weighted average cannot exceed its largest entry. Equality at q1 proves global optimality.
What if the eigenvalues tie?
Change to an isotropic cloud. Rotate freely.
All directions in a tied eigenspace give the same variance. A unique PC1 is not guaranteed.
Find the next component
Restrict the next direction to the perpendicular space.
Maximize remaining variance there. In two dimensions the remaining axis is fixed up to sign.
Read the PCA coordinates
Rotate both axes, then relabel the plot as PC1 and PC2.
Loadings describe axes. Scores describe observations.
Check the new covariance
Select an entry of QᵀSQ. See the off-diagonal product sum vanish.
The score columns are uncorrelated. This does not generally mean independent.
Explain the 90 percent
Connect eigenvalue bars to the sum of squared centered distances.
6/(6+2/3)=90%. This is a fraction of variance, not prediction accuracy.
Rebuild an observation from its score
Select A. Multiply its score by q1, then add the mean.
The reconstructed point lies on the retained line.
Draw the missing part
Show the original vector, projection, and residual as a right triangle.
Orthogonality gives original squared length = kept squared length + lost squared length.
Prove the second objective
Add the triangle identity across all observations.
Total squared length is fixed, so maximizing kept variance minimizes squared reconstruction error.
Recover both coordinates
Switch between k=0, k=1, and k=2.
Two orthonormal coordinates recover the original centered vector.
Choose how much to keep
Set a retained-variance target and select k.
The task determines an acceptable error. A percentage alone does not prove usefulness.
Extend from two features to p
Keep the top k eigenvalues in a larger spectrum.
For orthonormal W, retained variance is tr(WᵀSW). The top k eigenvectors maximize it; discarded eigenvalues give the loss.
Connect the result to SVD
Substitute Xc=UΣVᵀ into S=XcᵀXc/(n−1).
The columns of V are PCA directions. Eigenvalues equal squared singular values divided by n−1.
Use the axes on a new observation
Enter a new observation and apply the training mean and axes.
Fit preprocessing and PCA on training data. Reuse those values for later observations.
Decide what units mean
Change one feature scale, then compare standardization.
Standardization changes the question. It gives each nonconstant feature unit variance.
Large variance is not always useful
Reveal a distant observation and then category labels.
Outliers can dominate squared spread. A useful label can lie in a low-variance direction.
A line cannot follow every shape
Compare a ring with the elongated cloud.
PCA is linear. Two components may be necessary even if a curve has one intrinsic parameter.
